title: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, return the index where the target is found. If it is not found, return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted. Run in logarithmic time.
shortTitle: Search Insert Position — Find Where a Target Would Be Inserted

s1_definition.profdef: Search insert position is a binary search that returns the index of the target if present, or otherwise the lower-bound index, the first position whose element is greater than or equal to the target. When the loop terminates without a match, the low pointer naturally rests at exactly that insertion point, so we return low. It runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank keeps interest-rate tiers sorted ascending. When a new rate comes in, the clerk must slot it into the correct position so the list stays sorted. He binary-searches for the rate; if it already exists he returns that slot, and if not, the search naturally stops at the exact gap where the new rate belongs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary search, and when it ends without a match, low is exactly where the target should be inserted.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Search insert position is a binary search that returns the index of the target if present, or otherwise the lower-bound index, the first position whose element is greater than or equal to the target. When the loop terminates without a match, the low pointer naturally rests at exactly that insertion point, so we return low. It runs in O(log n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank keeps interest-rate tiers sorted ascending. When a new rate comes in, the clerk must slot it into the correct position so the list stays sorted. He binary-searches for the rate; if it already exists he returns that slot, and if not, the search naturally stops at the exact gap where the new rate belongs.

**One line to remember:** Binary search, and when it ends without a match, low is exactly where the target should be inserted.

sections.s2_technical:
This is classic binary search with one twist: instead of returning minus one on failure, we return the insertion index, which turns out to be the final value of low.

The loop is the familiar shape: `int low = 0, high = arr.length - 1; while (low <= high) { int mid = low + (high - low) / 2; if (arr[mid] == target) return mid; else if (arr[mid] < target) low = mid + 1; else high = mid - 1; } return low;`.

The reason low is the answer is the loop invariant. Throughout the search, every element before low is strictly less than the target and every element from high plus one onward is greater than the target. When low exceeds high the two bounds cross, and low points at the first element that is greater than or equal to the target, which is precisely where the target should go to preserve sorted order.

This handles all edges automatically. If the target is smaller than everything, low stays 0 and we insert at the front. If the target is larger than everything, low advances past the end to arr.length, meaning append at the back. If the target equals an element, we return early with that index.

A senior-level nuance is recognizing this as the lower-bound primitive. The same return-low pattern is the building block for insertion into sorted structures, for counting elements less than a value, and for binary-search-on-answer templates. Understanding why low is the insertion point, rather than memorizing it, lets you adapt the template confidently.

Another nuance is the overflow-safe midpoint, the same low plus high-minus-low over two, which stays correct for very large arrays.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India maintains a sorted list of interest-rate tier thresholds. When a new threshold is defined or a lookup is performed, the system must find where a given rate sits so it can either read the existing tier or insert the new threshold while keeping the list sorted. This is exactly the search-insert-position problem.

Problem 2 — Tier lists change over time and lookups are frequent, so the position must be found logarithmically rather than by scanning, and the same routine must serve both the found case and the not-found insertion case.

Problem 3 — Edge cases matter: a rate below all tiers inserts at the front, and a rate above all tiers inserts at the end, both of which the return-low behavior handles without special code.

In the code: a `RateTierService` holds a sorted int array of rate thresholds. A `search` method returns the found or insertion index. A `RateTierDemo` main checks an existing threshold, a middle gap, a below-all value, and an above-all value.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: tiers 300, 500, 700, 900 (indices 0 to 3).

Case 700 (exists): low 0 high 3 mid 1, arr[1] is 500 less, low becomes 2. low 2 high 3 mid 2, arr[2] is 700 match, return 2.

Case 600 (gap): low 0 high 3 mid 1, 500 less, low 2. low 2 high 3 mid 2, 700 greater, high 1. Now low 2 exceeds high 1, loop ends, return low which is 2. Inserting at 2 keeps order 300, 500, 600, 700, 900.

Case 100 (below all): every comparison pushes high down. low stays 0, loop ends, return 0, insert at front.

Case 1000 (above all): every comparison pushes low up. low reaches 4, loop ends, return 4, append at back.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Position for existing threshold 700
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Index -> 2
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Position to insert new threshold 600 (gap)
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Index -> 2
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Position to insert threshold 100 (below all)
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Index -> 0
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Position to insert threshold 1000 (above all)
2026-10-26 22:20:00 [INFO] Index -> 4
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [300 500 700 900]

    ├─ target 700 → mid1<→low2 ; mid2 match → return 2
    ├─ target 600 → mid1<→low2 ; mid2>→high1 ; low>high → return low=2
    ├─ target 100 → all > → high shrinks to -1 → return low=0 (front)
    └─ target 1000→ all < → low grows to 4 → return low=4 (append)
    ▼
  Output: low is always the sorted insertion position
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Search insert position is ordinary binary search with one small but important change: instead of returning minus one when the target is not present, I return the final value of the low pointer, which is exactly the position where the target should be inserted to keep the array sorted. The reason this works is the loop invariant, because throughout the search every element before low is strictly less than the target and every element from high plus one onward is greater, so when low and high cross, low rests on the first element greater than or equal to the target, which is the correct insertion point.

What I like about this is that it handles every edge case with no special code. If the target is smaller than everything, low never moves and I insert at the front. If it is larger than everything, low walks all the way to the array length and I append at the back. If it matches an existing element, I return that index early. This is the lower-bound primitive, and recognizing it as such means I can reuse the same template for counting how many elements are below a value or for inserting into any sorted structure.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, we keep interest-rate tier thresholds in a sorted list. When a new threshold is defined or a rate is looked up, this routine finds where it sits so the system either reads the matching tier or inserts the new threshold while preserving sorted order, all in logarithmic time rather than by scanning the list.

The two details I always keep correct are the overflow-safe midpoint computation and understanding why low, not high, is the insertion index. Memorizing return low is fragile, but understanding the invariant that drives it means I can derive and adapt the template under interview pressure without second-guessing myself.
